                                         significantly enhanced the visual grounding task, which in-                                                          VLM

                                         volves locating objects in an image based on natural lan-
                                         guage queries. Despite these advancements, the secu-
                                         rity of VLM-based grounding systems has not been thor-
                                         oughly investigated. This paper reveals a novel and re-
                                         alistic vulnerability: the first multi-target backdoor attack
                                         on VLM-based visual grounding. Unlike prior attacks that

Figure 2. Overall framework of the proposed IAG. First, the trigger generator (text-conditioned UNet) generates a trigger based on the
benign image and text guidance of any attack target object in the image by the frozen benign embedding layer. The trigger is a gray-looking
pattern, whose size is the same as the benign image’s. Second, the trigger is added onto the benign image to construct a triggered image.
Then it is fed into the VLM. After joint-training of the UNet and the VLM, the backdoored VLM will generate the location of the attack
target object. Once deployed on downstream tasks, this will become an emergent security issue.

within the image. (2) Backdoor injection involves embed-                   To further ensure that the trigger remains imperceptible

    Poison rate. Figure 4 illustrates the performance of IAG             In this paper, we propose IAG, a novel input-aware back-
at poison rates of 1%, 5%, and 10%. It shows that even with              door attack against VLM-based visual grounding. IAG uti-
a very low poison rate (1%), IAG can reach an ASR@0.5                    lizes a text-conditioned U-Net to generate dynamic, text-
only about 5% lower than primary results. A higher poison                guided triggers that can manipulate grounding outputs to-
rate brings slight increase in attack performance. This sug-             ward any attacker-specified object in the input image, all
gests that even small-scale poisoning is sufficient to attack,           while maintaining performance on benign samples. Com-
underscoring the effectiveness of IAG at low poison rates.               prehensive experiments across multiple VLMs and datasets
    Time consumption. To evaluate the efficiency of IAG                  confirm its effectiveness, stealthiness, and unnoticeability.
attack, we test the time consumption at inference time of                Notably, IAG remains robust under various defense strate-
across three VLMs. Specifically, we randomly sample 10                   gies and performs well even under low poison rates, trans-
questions from used datasets, ensuring similar context to-               ferring scenarios and real-world conditions. We hope this
ken lengths, both with and without attack targets. For each              work sparks further attention to the overlooked security
instance, we record the inference time and report the mean               risks in grounding-capable VLMs.

    Regarding a corner case, in evaluation, when specifying
a non-existent object in the image, VLMs’ grounding accu-
racies dropped largely, with a decline of over 50 percent-
age points on all datasets tested. This finding strongly
contradicts the “object detector” hypothesis: unlike a detec-
tor which fails without the object, IAG generates effective           Attack Target Sentence: AntiVirus
triggers even for absent targets, causing semantic shifts and         Model answer: virus pic[[168,88,671,634]]
forcing the VLM to hallucinate (dropping accuracy).

Q. Real-world Evaluation
We captured photographs and screenshots of real-world sce-
narios to assess whether attackers can manipulate real ex-
amples using one of the backdoored VLMs: InternVL-2.5-
8B, trained on RefCoco with a poison rate of 0.05. Be-
low are some examples. The green box indicates the user-
required ground truth, while the red box represents the at-
tack target. In Case 1, we find that attackers can select mul-        Attack Target Sentence: bottom left news

S. Ethical Consideration
This research highlights security vulnerabilities in AI mod-
els, specifically focusing on backdoor attacks. While our
goal is to improve security of model use, we recognize that
exposing these vulnerabilities could also facilitate misuse.
We are committed to sharing our findings responsibly, en-
suring transparency in our methods and limiting access to
sensitive materials.
   We use publicly available datasets, and we adhere to eth-
ical guidelines to prevent harm. Our work also acknowl-
edges the potential risks in VLMs, and we aim to evaluate
and mitigate any unintended impacts on fairness.
   Finally, we emphasize the importance of human over-
sight, transparency, and post-deployment monitoring in AI
systems to ensure that our methods contribute to secure and
ethical AI development.
